entries.referenceAnswer: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent, and it's the philosophy behind many distributed NoSQL systems. Instead of guaranteeing that every read sees the latest write, like ACID, a BASE system stays available and accepts writes even when replicas can't talk to each other, and promises only that the replicas will eventually agree once updates stop. For example, when you like a post, a friend on another server might see the old like count for a second or two. That's fine for likes, view counts or feeds, and it lets the system scale across data centres. It's not fine for a bank balance or seat booking, where you need ACID's immediate consistency.
commonMistakes: Saying eventual consistency means data may be lost
Saying BASE is simply the opposite of ACID with no trade-off reasoning

entries.concept: OLTP vs OLAP and data warehouses
questions: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
What is a star schema?
keyPoints: OLTP (online transaction processing): many small, fast read/write transactions on current data (orders, payments); normalized schema; row-oriented storage
OLAP (online analytical processing): complex read-heavy queries aggregating large amounts of historical data (reports, dashboards)
OLAP data usually lives in a data warehouse, loaded from OLTP systems via ETL/ELT
Star schema: a central fact table (measurable events, e.g. sales) with foreign keys to denormalized dimension tables (date, product, store)
Snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions further
Columnar storage suits OLAP because queries read a few columns across many rows
entries.referenceAnswer: OLTP systems run the business day to day: lots of small, fast transactions like placing an order or updating a balance, on current data, with a normalized schema to keep writes consistent. OLAP systems are for analysis: fewer but much heavier queries that scan and aggregate years of history, like total sales per region per quarter. Running those on the production database would slow it down, so data is copied through ETL into a separate data warehouse designed for reading. There the typical design is a star schema: a central fact table of events, like each sale with its amount, surrounded by dimension tables for date, product, customer and store. Warehouses often use columnar storage, since analytical queries read a few columns across millions of rows.
commonMistakes: Saying OLAP systems should be highly normalized
Confusing fact tables with dimension tables

questions: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: One query fetches a list of N parent records, then one additional query is run per record to fetch related data: N+1 queries
Common with ORMs and lazy loading, e.g. loading posts then each post's author inside a loop
Each query has network round-trip overhead, so it gets very slow as N grows
Fix with eager loading: a JOIN, or a single batched query with WHERE id IN (...)
ORM tools: Mongoose populate (batches into one $in query), Sequelize include, JPA JOIN FETCH, Django select_related/prefetch_related
Detect it by logging queries or using query-count monitoring
entries.referenceAnswer: The N+1 problem is when code runs one query to get a list, then another query for each item in it. For example, fetch 100 blog posts, then loop over them and fetch each author separately: 101 queries, each paying a network round trip, when two would do. It usually sneaks in through ORMs with lazy loading, where post.author looks like a simple property access but hides a query. The fix is to load related data in bulk: either join the tables in one query, or collect all the author IDs and fetch them with a single WHERE id IN (...) query. Most ORMs have eager-loading options for this, like populate in Mongoose or include in Sequelize. You spot it by logging queries and noticing the same query repeated with different IDs.
commonMistakes: Thinking more small queries are cheaper than one join
Not being able to name a fix

questions: What is database connection pooling and why is it needed?
keyPoints: Opening a database connection is expensive: TCP handshake, authentication, TLS, server-side memory per connection
A connection pool keeps a set of open connections that requests borrow and return
Removes connection setup cost from every request, so latency drops
Caps the number of connections so the database isn't overwhelmed
Settings: minimum/maximum pool size, idle timeout, wait timeout when all connections are busy
Most drivers/ORMs pool by default (e.g. the MongoDB driver used by Mongoose, pg Pool)
entries.referenceAnswer: Creating a database connection is surprisingly expensive: a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication, and the database allocating memory for a session. Doing that for every web request would add a lot of latency and could overwhelm the database under load. A connection pool opens a set of connections once and keeps them alive. Each request borrows a connection, uses it and returns it to the pool. That removes setup cost from the request path and also limits the total number of connections, which protects the database. If all connections are busy, new requests wait for one to free up, up to a timeout. Most drivers do this by default. The MongoDB driver under Mongoose, for instance, keeps a pool, which is why you connect once at startup rather than per request.
commonMistakes: Opening a new connection per request
Thinking a bigger pool is always better (the database has limits)

questions: What are generalization and specialization in an ER model?
How would you map an Employee superclass with Engineer and Manager subclasses into tables?
keyPoints: Specialization (top-down): defining subclasses of an entity with extra attributes (Employee to Engineer, Manager)
Generalization (bottom-up): combining entities with common attributes into a superclass (Car, Bike to Vehicle)
Subclasses inherit the superclass's attributes and relationships
Constraints: disjoint vs overlapping; total vs partial participation

Mapping options: single table with a type column (simple, many NULLs); a table per subclass sharing the primary key of the superclass table (normalized, needs joins); a table per concrete class (no joins, duplicated columns)
entries.referenceAnswer: Specialization works top-down: you start from a general entity like Employee and define subtypes, like Engineer with a programming language and Manager with a budget. Generalization is the bottom-up version: you notice Car and Bike share attributes and pull them into a Vehicle superclass. Subtypes inherit the parent's attributes, and you specify whether an entity can belong to several subtypes (overlapping) or just one (disjoint), and whether every entity must belong to some subtype. To map it to tables there are three common options. One table for everything, with a type column, is simple but leaves many NULL columns. One table for Employee plus one per subtype, sharing the primary key, is clean and normalized but needs joins. Or one table per concrete subtype repeating the common columns, which avoids joins but duplicates structure.
commonMistakes: Mixing up which direction is generalization and which is specialization
Not knowing any mapping strategy

questions: What is table partitioning? What is the difference between horizontal and vertical partitioning?
How is partitioning different from sharding?
keyPoints: Partitioning splits one large table into smaller pieces that are managed separately
Horizontal partitioning: split rows (by range, e.g. per month; by list; or by hash)
Vertical partitioning: split columns, e.g. moving rarely used or large columns into another table
Partition pruning: queries only scan the relevant partitions, e.g. only this month's
Makes maintenance easier: drop an old partition instead of deleting millions of rows
Sharding is horizontal partitioning across different servers; plain partitioning usually stays within one database server
entries.referenceAnswer: Partitioning splits a huge table into smaller pieces while it still looks like one table to queries. Horizontal partitioning divides the rows, for example an orders table split by month, or by a hash of the customer ID. Vertical partitioning divides the columns, for example moving big or rarely used columns like a profile description into a separate table so the main table stays compact. The big benefit is partition pruning: a query for last week's orders only touches that partition instead of scanning years of data. Maintenance also gets easier, since archiving old data means dropping a partition instead of running a massive DELETE. Sharding is essentially horizontal partitioning taken across multiple servers, while ordinary partitioning keeps all the pieces inside one database server.
commonMistakes: Swapping horizontal and vertical partitioning
Treating partitioning and sharding as identical
